title: Al-Nakira wa-l-Maʿrifa (the Indefinite and the Definite Noun)

sections.text: Al-Nakira wa-l-Maʿrifa (the Indefinite and the Definite Noun)

With respect to how it points to its referent, the noun is of two kinds: indefinite (nakira) and definite (maʿrifa). The indefinite denotes something unspecified; the definite denotes something specific in itself.

If you say 'a man came' (jaʾa rajul), you are reporting about a man the listener does not identify in particular — that is indefinite. If you say 'Muhammad came' (jaʾa Muhammad), you have specified the one meant, so the listener identifies him — that is definite. Nouns are originally indefinite and are then made definite by one of the means of definiteness.
First: The Indefinite (Al-Nakira)
The indefinite noun denotes something unspecified, common to its whole class and not restricted to one instance rather than another — e.g. rajul (a man), kitab (a book), madina (a city).
The mark of the indefinite: it accepts the definite article 'al-' which makes it definite — rajul → al-rajul, kitab → al-kitab. Many indefinites also accept tanwin (the tanwin of indefiniteness).

items.text: — In the garden is a beautiful bird.
— I sat with a man on the road.

sections.text: The words 'kitaban', 'taʾirun', and 'rajulin' are indefinite, because none denotes a specific thing in itself, and 'al-' may be added to them so that you say al-kitab, al-taʾir, al-rajul — turning them into definites.
Second: The Definite (Al-Maʿrifa)
The definite noun denotes a specific thing in itself that the addressee identifies — e.g. ana (I), Muhammad, hadha (this), alladhi (the one who), al-kitab (the book).

The words 'al-kitaba', 'Muhammadun', and 'hadha' are definite, because each denotes something specific that the listener identifies; so one cannot ask about them with 'which?' (ayy) as one asks about the indefinite.
Types of Definite Nouns

The definites are seven types: the pronoun (damir), the proper name (ʿalam), the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), the relative noun (al-ism al-mawsul), the noun made definite by 'al-', the noun annexed to one of these definites, and the intended-particular vocative (al-munada al-nakira al-maqsuda).

items: Pronoun: ana, nahnu, huwa, the 'ta' in katabtu.
Made definite by 'al-': al-kitab, al-shams, al-qamar.
Annexed to a definite: kitabu Muhammad, babu al-madrasa.
Intended vocative: ya rajul (to a particular man).

sections.text: 1 — The Pronoun (Al-Damir)
The pronoun is a definite that denotes a speaker (ana, nahnu), an addressee (anta, anti), or an absent third party (huwa, hiya). It is the most definite of all the definites.

rows: Pronounced independently; may begin a sentence
the 'ta' in katabtu, the 'ka' in kitabuka, the 'ha' in raʾaytuhu
Not pronounced independently; joins the end of a word
understood as 'ana' in aktubu, 'anta' in uktub, 'huwa' in yaktubu
Appears neither in speech nor in writing

sections.text: In the first example 'ana' is a detached pronoun of the speaker; in the second the 'ta' is an attached pronoun in the position of subject; in the third the subject is a concealed pronoun understood as 'huwa' referring to the teacher.
2 — The Proper Name (Al-ʿAlam)
The proper name denotes something specific in itself without any contextual indicator, and it includes names of persons, lands, rivers, and so on — e.g. Muhammad, Makka, al-Nil (the Nile).

items.text: — Khalid conquered many of the lands.

sections.text: 3 — The Demonstrative (Ism al-Ishara)
The demonstrative is a definite by which one points to something specific — physically or figuratively — distinguishing it from others, e.g. hadha, hadhihi, dhalika, ulaʾika.
4 — The Relative Noun (Al-Ism al-Mawsul)
The relative noun does not complete its reference to something specific except by a clause coming after it, called the relative clause (silat al-mawsul) — e.g. alladhi, allati, alladhina, man, ma.

items.text: — The one who worked hard succeeded.
— I respect the one (f.) who is truthful in her speech.
— Honour whoever has been good to you.

sections.text: 5 — Made Definite by 'Al-'

The article 'al-' is prefixed to an indefinite and makes it definite — qalam → al-qalam, shams → al-shams. It is either 'ʿahdiyya' (referring to a known particular) or 'jinsiyya' (denoting the whole class).

In the last example, 'al-insan' takes the generic 'al-' (jinsiyya) denoting the whole class, not one particular individual; whereas in the second example 'al-madrasa' takes the 'ahdiyya' article referring to a school known to both speaker and listener.
6 — Made Definite by Annexation (Idafa)

When an indefinite is annexed to a definite, it acquires definiteness from it and becomes definite — 'kitab' is indefinite, but when you say 'kitabu Muhammad' (Muhammad's book), 'kitab' becomes definite through its acquisition from 'Muhammad'.

items.text: — I opened the door of the school.

sections.text: The words 'bab', 'kitab', and 'sadiq' are originally indefinite, but they acquired definiteness by being annexed to the definites after them: 'al-madrasa' (definite by al-), 'al-tarikh' (definite by al-), and 'akhi' (definite by annexation to the speaker's pronoun).
7 — The Intended-Particular Vocative (Al-Munada al-Nakira al-Maqsuda)

An indefinite that is intended particularly in a call becomes definite, because the speaker meant a specific one by it — as when you say to a particular man 'ya rajul aqbil' (O man, come here); the call and the intent have made it definite.

'Talib' and 'rajul' are originally indefinite, but once a particular person is intended by them in the call they become definite; that is why they are built on damma in the position of the accusative.
The Ranks of the Definites

The definites vary in the strength of their definiteness: the most definite is the pronoun, then the proper name, then the demonstrative, then the relative noun, then the noun made definite by 'al-', then the noun annexed to a definite — whose strength follows that of what it is annexed to.
What is the benefit of knowing the difference between the indefinite and the definite in iʿrab and meaning?

Its benefit is that many grammatical rulings are built on this distinction: the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ) is in principle only a definite or something close to it; the circumstantial accusative (hal) is only indefinite; the adjective (naʿt) follows its noun in definiteness and indefiniteness; and a clause after an indefinite is an adjective while after a definite it is a hal. Whoever cannot tell the indefinite from the definite will get much of the iʿrab wrong.

sections.text: Not every noun that takes 'al-' becomes definite; 'al-' may be redundant and give no definiteness, as in some proper names: al-Harith, al-ʿAbbas, al-Fadl. Likewise the annexed noun does not acquire definiteness unless it is annexed to a definite; if it is annexed to an indefinite it stays indefinite, e.g. 'babu dar' (a door of a house).
A Full Iʿrab Model

hadha: a demonstrative, built on sukun, in the position of nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ); it is definite. kitabu: the predicate, nominative with a visible damma; it is a mudaf (first term of annexation) and acquired definiteness by annexation to 'Muhammad'. Muhammadin: the mudaf ilayh, genitive with a visible kasra; it is a proper name and definite.
God Most High said: ﴿al-hamdu li-llahi rabbi al-ʿalamin﴾ — 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.'

In this noble verse several types of definite come together: 'al-hamd' is made definite by 'al-'; 'Allah' is a proper name of the Divine Essence; 'rabb' is a mudaf that acquired definiteness by annexation to 'al-ʿalamin'; and 'al-ʿalamin' is made definite by 'al-'.
And He said: ﴿qala hadha rabbi﴾ — 'He said: This is my Lord.'

In His words 'hadha' is a demonstrative, definite, in the position of nominative as subject; 'rabbi' is the predicate, nominative, a mudaf that acquired definiteness by annexation to the speaker's 'ya' (a pronoun, definite). So two types of definite meet in the sentence: the demonstrative and the noun annexed to a pronoun.
